text: Patagonia's "Don't Buy This Jacket" campaign ran a full-page ad in The New York Times on Black Friday 2011 asking customers to think twice before purchasing. The image showed the company's R2 fleece with a caption explaining the environmental cost of producing it: 135 liters of water per jacket, twenty-four times its weight in carbon dioxide, two-thirds the journey from the source to the warehouse using fossil fuels. The campaign positioned consumption itself as the brand's antagonist, building loyalty through honesty about scale rather than aspiration about lifestyle.

Aesop, the Australian skincare brand, designs every retail store as a one-off architectural collaboration. The Soho store has a wall of stacked printing-press drawers; the Tribeca store is lined with floor-to-ceiling shelves of Penguin Classics paperbacks. Products sit on butcher block and unfinished pine. The packaging is brown amber glass with typography set in Optima — a serif from 1958 that reads as scholarly rather than clinical. The brand never lists active ingredients on the front; the front carries only a product number and a line of body copy.

The Dollar Shave Club launch video in 2012 cost roughly $4,500 and was shot in a single afternoon. CEO Michael Dubin walks through the company warehouse delivering deadpan one-liners about overpriced razors. Within forty-eight hours of going live, the site had 12,000 orders. The video worked because it diagnosed an irritation customers had not yet articulated to themselves — that razor cartridges were a quietly extracted tax — and gave them a culprit and a relief in the same ninety seconds.

Mailchimp's brand voice guide instructs writers to be 'plain but never plain.' Examples included in the guide: avoid 'utilize' (use 'use'), avoid 'leverage' (use 'use'), avoid 'streamline' (just say what improves). The mascot Freddie is a winking chimp with a postal cap, drawn by a small in-house team since 2003. The brand has resisted modernizing him through several rebrands because the slight wonkiness signals that the product is run by humans, not by a private-equity-owned platform.

REI closed all 143 of its stores on Black Friday 2015 and paid 12,000 employees to spend the day outside. The campaign hashtag #OptOutside became the only website at rei.com for twenty-four hours. Membership grew by a million in the year that followed. The campaign worked because it stated, in operational rather than rhetorical form, that the cooperative's stakeholders were members and employees rather than quarterly revenue — and made that claim hard to back out of in subsequent years.

The Method dish soap bottle, designed by Karim Rashid, sits on the counter like a sculpture rather than hiding under the sink. The teardrop silhouette and pump (rather than squeeze) head made the product part of kitchen decor for a generation of urban renters who had no countertop space to waste on hiding ugly cleaning supplies. The packaging carries the company's manifesto in small type on the back: 'People against dirty.' The brand was acquired by SC Johnson in 2017 for an undisclosed sum reported to be above one billion dollars.

Liquid Death is canned mountain water sold in tall-boy aluminum cans designed to look like craft beer. The brand was founded in 2019 by a former creative director at Netflix who noticed that nightclubs were the most reliable channel for selling sober beverages: a person carrying a can looks like everyone else, which removes the social tax on not drinking. The marketing is built around heavy-metal aesthetics, mock-violent ad copy ('Murder Your Thirst'), and a death-metal-styled brand voice that makes a commodity product memorable by giving it an unmistakable signature.

Brandy Melville sells nearly its entire catalog in 'one size fits most.' The strategy is widely criticized as exclusionary, but the company built a multi-billion-dollar business by treating its stores as physical Instagram feeds: every fixture is photogenic, the lighting is engineered for selfies, employees are recruited as models. The brand's growth came not from advertising but from the user-generated content of the stores themselves circulating on social media. There is no e-commerce expansion strategy because the constraint is the marketing engine.

Yeti Coolers built its brand by selling $400 coolers to fishing guides and hunting outfitters who needed equipment that could survive twenty seasons of abuse. The earliest marketing was sponsorships of professional anglers and a long-form magazine — Yeti Stories — that ran multi-thousand-word features on the cultures of bowhunters, barbecue pitmasters, and rodeo bullfighters. The company did not advertise on price for the first decade. The brand premium was built by consistently treating the customer as a craftsperson and the product as a craftperson's tool.

The Allbirds wool runner was launched in 2016 with a single SKU in three colors. The shoe was constructed of merino wool sourced from New Zealand, with a sole made from sugar-cane-derived EVA foam. The packaging was a single recycled fiber box that doubled as the shipping container. The brand grew by avoiding the conventions of athletic-shoe marketing — no athlete endorsements, no performance claims, no seasonal drops — and instead positioning the product as a uniform: one shoe, worn every day, for people who do not want to think about shoes.

Glossier started as the comments section of Into the Gloss, a beauty blog founded by Emily Weiss in 2010. When the blog launched its own product line in 2014 with a four-product Phase One Set, the products were designed in response to threads where readers had described what they wanted but could not buy. The Boy Brow eyebrow gel, the Balm Dotcom universal salve, and the Milky Jelly face wash were all named in plain language and packaged in millennial pink. The brand's first store, on Lafayette Street in SoHo, was designed to feel like the inside of a friend's bathroom.

Warby Parker's Home Try-On program — five frames shipped to your house, free returns — solved a single overlooked friction in online eyewear: people cannot decide what looks good on their own face without seeing it on their own face. The program was operationally expensive, but the per-customer acquisition cost ended up lower than paid digital advertising because each box turned the buyer's home into a small trial showroom shared with family and roommates. The company also paired every purchase with a donation of a pair of glasses, building a give-one-get-one frame around a category that had previously had no narrative at all.

The Oatly carton was redesigned in 2015 by John Schoolcraft. The new packaging carried long, conversational paragraphs of body copy across the front and sides of the carton, written in the voice of the company itself — self-aware, irritable about milk industry lobbying, willing to argue with the reader on the carton itself. The redesign treated the package as the company's primary media channel. The strategy moved oat milk from a niche allergen substitute into the default plant-based alternative at coffee shops across Europe and North America within five years.

Casper's launch in 2014 sold one mattress, in one firmness, shipped in a box, with a one-hundred-night return policy. The unit economics worked because the firm replaced the cost of retail floor space and outside sales commissions with the cost of warehousing returns and reselling them as refurbished units. The marketing — subway car wraps, podcast read sponsorships, a content site called Van Winkle's — leaned on the brand voice of a smart insomniac friend explaining mattresses to you because the rest of the industry would not.

Lush Cosmetics sells its products unpackaged whenever possible. Solid shampoo bars sit in baskets on counters; bath bombs are stacked like fruit at a market. The retail staff are trained to demonstrate products on customers' hands within thirty seconds of entry — the rationale being that the sensory experience does the selling. The brand was built without paid advertising for its first twenty years. Each store carries a manifesto card listing the company's positions: against animal testing, against excess packaging, in favor of fair trade, in favor of fresh ingredients with handwritten use-by dates.

Headspace built its meditation app on the voice of co-founder Andy Puddicombe — a former Buddhist monk with a measured, gently authoritative tone that made guided meditation accessible to listeners who had been put off by either New Age earnestness or clinical mindfulness language. The product's first marketing was a series of short, hand-illustrated animations explaining concepts like equanimity and impermanence in two minutes. The brand grew not by acquiring users through paid channels but by being recommended inside companies as part of employee benefit packages, which turned the app into infrastructure rather than a personal purchase.

Trader Joe's does no broadcast advertising and runs no loyalty program. The Fearless Flyer — a print newsletter dropped at every store and mailed to customers who request it — is the company's principal marketing channel. It is written in a faux-1950s broadsheet voice with illustrated product descriptions; new items are announced as if they are minor news events. The chain rotates twenty percent of its SKU base every year, which creates urgency without discounting. The voice and the curation together make a grocery store feel like a magazine you visit weekly.

The Hims and Hers launch in 2017 packaged generic finasteride, sildenafil, and minoxidil — drugs available at any pharmacy — as a subscription experience for men who would not previously have asked their primary care doctor about hair loss or erectile dysfunction. The marketing was full-color subway car wraps showing a single wilting cactus or a withered houseplant with a one-word caption. The strategy worked by giving an embarrassing transaction the affordances of a luxury subscription: doorstep delivery, a clean web flow, no in-person interaction with a pharmacist or a clinician.

Duolingo's mascot — a green owl named Duo who sends mildly threatening notifications about your missed lessons — became the company's primary marketing asset on TikTok in 2021. The brand's social media manager treated the owl as a character with a chaotic, lovesick inner life rather than as a logo. The account routinely produces content that has nothing to do with language learning. The result is that the app is recommended by users for the personality of its mascot, which is a more durable acquisition channel than any paid campaign at scale.

Stripe's earliest marketing was a single line of code — seven lines, when announced in 2011 — that replaced the multi-week PCI compliance and merchant account setup that had previously been required to accept a credit card on the web. The company's documentation site was treated with the same care as its product: example code that runs, error messages that include the fix, a changelog written in plain English. The brand was built by being the first developer-facing product in payments that had taken the developer's time seriously enough to make the documentation feel like the user interface.
